accuracy.evidence: Maths checked against the National Curriculum (2013) Year 2–3 place value and column addition (exchange ten ones for one ten) and NCETM guidance on regrouping: 27 + 15 = 3 tens + 12 ones = 4 tens + 2 ones = 42. Multiplication facts checked: 6 × 3 = 18, 6 × 2 = 12, 6 × 1 = 6, 6 × 0 = 0, 6 × ½ = 3; 'multiplying makes bigger' holds only for multipliers greater than 1. Array split k × 8 + (7 − k) × 8 = 56 for every k = 1–6 (distributive property). Science reasons are correct at this level (evaporation, light blocked by an opaque object, plants use light to make food, gravity). The strategy claims follow Dunlosky et al. (2013) on elaborative interrogation and self-explanation and the EEF metacognition guidance.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: treating the carried 1 as one (not one ten), carrying when fewer than ten ones are left, over-generalising 'multiplication makes bigger' (well documented in research on multiplicative reasoning), and accepting authority, rule-based or circular statements as explanations. The sorter and challenge feedback name each of these.

lab_distinct.evidence: Each activity asks 'why?' about a real mechanism: bundling ones into a ten, testing a rule until it breaks, sorting fact / real why / fake why, rebuilding a forgotten fact by splitting an array, and linking new ideas to old. Teaching It Back (flagteach) is about explaining to a toy and finding gaps; Knowing what you don't know (flagcalib) is about confidence. No other flagship has a rule-breaker scale or fake-reason sorter; the shingle gate passed against all flag_*.js files.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees the carried 1 become a ten, then sees that a rule known without its reason fails for ×1, ×0 and ×½, then learns to tell a real reason from a fake one, then uses understanding to rebuild 7 × 8 two ways, and finally links new ideas to old ones. This matches the topic evidence: asks why, explains the reason behind a rule (carrying the ten), and connects new to known.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: the carried 1 is worth '1' (disproved when ten ones become one ten rod), '6 × ½ is bigger because multiplying makes bigger' (disproved on the scale), and 'Yes, it has because' for 'because that is the rule' (disproved by the sorter).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating 'which answer really explains why?' questions with six distinct m= messages: circular reason, authority ('the teacher told me', 'the answer book'), 'it is a rule', the multiplication myth, an irrelevant true fact, and the correct answer explained.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete examples (puddles, carrying, 7 × 8) within the family kid limit. Adult text names the terms procedural and conceptual understanding, regrouping (exchanging), elaborative interrogation, self-explanation and metacognition within the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and 12% duplicate gate. Kid text covers fact versus reason, asking why, fake reasons and the payoff; adult text covers the concept, the research-backed strategy, the two common mistakes and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android and iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark for all six steps: the rule-breaker counter overlapped the 6 label and the third sorter bin title clipped, so the counter moved under the rule and the bins became Fact / Real why / Fake why. Ten-frame, rods, array and idea cards all fit and stay readable.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes, no console errors. Every drag has a button route (move a one, 6 × each number, bin buttons, split-after-row buttons, old-idea buttons) and the canvas aria-label reports each result.
